## 391135: bipartite list-coloring, three sustained approaches

Fix an integer k>=1. A finite bipartite graph on parts L,R can be completed to K_{a,b} without adding vertices. A list assignment not colorable on the original graph stays not colorable after adding edges. Conversely K_{a,b} itself is an allowed graph. Thus the minimum order is achieved by a complete bipartite obstruction. Isolated vertices cause no problem for k>=1; an edgeless graph is colorable.

For k-element lists (S_l) and (T_r), colorability of K_{a,b} is equivalent to existence of a subset X of the finite union of all lists such that every S_l meets X and every T_r meets its complement. Forward: take X to be the colors actually used on L. None is used on R because every cross pair is adjacent. Backward: independently choose a color in S_l intersect X and T_r outside X. Same-part repetitions are allowed. This proves an exact reduction to two-family separation, including unequal side sizes and repeated lists. It does NOT determine the minimum a+b.

First route, random palette separation: place each color in X independently with probability 1/2. Each left list misses X with probability 2^{-k}; each right list is contained in X with the same probability. The union bound gives a coloring whenever a+b<2^k. For k>=2 and a+b=2^k, if either part has at least two vertices, its corresponding two bad events have positive intersection (all colors outside X for two left lists, or inside X for two right lists). The pointwise bound for the union is at most the sum of indicators minus the indicator of that intersection. Therefore its probability is strictly less than (a+b)2^{-k}=1. At least one part has two vertices since 2^k>=4. Thus every bipartite graph with at most 2^k vertices is k-choosable for k>=2. This helper supplies n(k)>2^k, not the exact n(k) or tight polynomial factor. For k=1 the edge is a two-vertex obstruction and the equality argument does not apply.

Second route, property B: let m(k) be the least number of distinct k-sets having no subset meeting each set and its complement. Fewer than m(k) total lists have property B, so the same partition works for both sides and colors any bipartite graph. Hence n(k)>=m(k). Conversely take a non-property-B family F of size m(k), put a copy of every list on each side of K_{m(k),m(k)}. A proper coloring would produce X hitting every list on the left and its complement hitting every identical list on the right, a contradiction. Hence n(k)<=2m(k). No primary-source claim about the optimal constant or asymptotics is being imported. This exact bridge also shows why a small-list witness or a property-B construction alone does not settle all k.

Third route, biased palette optimization: at bias p the upper bound on failure becomes a(1-p)^k+b p^k. For k>1 its interior minimum has p/(1-p)=(a/b)^{1/(k-1)}, by equating derivatives (a,b>0). With x=a^{1/(k-1)}, y=b^{1/(k-1)}, the minimum is (xy/(x+y))^{k-1}. This improves the sufficient condition for highly unbalanced parts. It cannot establish necessity: the union bound discards correlations determined by overlapping lists. The exact missing step is a sharp lower bound on a+b for two families admitting no separator, together with a matching obstruction family for every k. ## 391147: cycles versus actual chords, three sustained approaches

Use the actual-graph convention: for a simple cycle C of length s, its chords are E(G[V(C)]) minus its s cycle edges. The prohibited configuration has |E(G[V(C)])|>=2s. A complete graph on the same vertex set is not implicitly present. This identity is elementary from the definition, not a theorem imported from the challenge-bearing webpage.

There is a concrete linear lower family. In K_{3,t}, every simple cycle alternates parts and has length 2r with 2<=r<=3. Its induced graph on those vertices has r^2 edges, hence r^2-2r chords. Since r<4, r^2-2r<2r. Thus every such cycle satisfies the strict condition. There are t+3 vertices and 3t=3n-9 edges for t>=1 (with no cycles when t=1). Any universal asymptotic linear upper constant is therefore at least 3. In K_{4,4}, an alternating Hamiltonian cycle has length 8 and 16-8=8 chords, violating the strict condition. This is a boundary illustration, not a counterexample to a linear upper bound.

First upper-bound attempt: peel a low-degree vertex and induct. A proof that every admissible graph has degree bounded by an absolute D in some nonempty induced subgraph would give e<=Dn. The condition is hereditary under deleting vertices and edges: each retained cycle has no additional chords. But the needed low-degree lemma has not been proved; the K_{3,t} examples show that D<3 cannot work in general. Density alone is not an induced Hamiltonian subgraph theorem.

Second attempt: let v1,...,vt be a longest path and let j be the largest index adjacent to v1. Every neighbor of v1 lies on that path. The cycle v1,...,vj,v1 has j vertices and exactly d(v1)-2 chords incident to v1. To reach j chords, one still needs at least j-d(v1)+2 chords among v2,...,vj. Longest-path maximality provides no such count. Raising the endpoint degree does not remove this deficit: d(v1)<=j-1. Longest-path endpoint rotation would need simultaneous control of internal chords across the rotated paths, not just many distinct endpoints. That is an unpaid combinatorial lemma.

Third attempt: choose a longest cycle and analyze outside attachments. An outside vertex cannot be adjacent to consecutive cycle vertices, since it would extend the cycle by one. This controls individual attachments but does not bound the total number of outside edges or the chords of a different cycle. In particular, many outside vertices may have the same allowed attachment pattern. Passing to a highly connected subgraph does not prove it Hamiltonian. The precise missing implication is an absolute density threshold forcing SOME simple cycle C with e(G[V(C)])>=2|C|. This remains the full upper-bound difficulty, not a paid consequence of minimum degree. ## 391112: arbitrary-index almost-disjoint family, three sustained approaches

For countably many infinite A_i there is a simple construction: at stage i choose two new points x_i,y_i of A_i, avoiding the finitely many earlier chosen points, and color x_i red, y_i blue. Extend arbitrarily to all remaining points. Each A_i has both colors. This uses neither finite intersections nor the no-singleton-intersection assumption. Finite families are handled identically. The full literal has no restriction on the number of indices; this helper is not a full answer.

First extension attempt, transfinite fresh pairs, fails at a genuine quantified step. After infinitely many earlier stages, the earlier chosen set can cover an entire countably infinite A_i. Pairwise finite intersections does not imply that the union of arbitrarily many such intersections is finite. It is invalid to replace that union by one finite intersection. A successful argument must either reuse already oppositely colored pairs or prove a suitable controlled-ordering lemma; neither is supplied by the literal.

Second extension attempt, compactness, does not work in the naive product space {0,1}^U. The requirement on A_i is an infinite union of cylinder sets asserting c(x)!=c(y). It is open, not necessarily closed. On U=N and A=N, color the first j points red and the rest blue. Every coloring is nonconstant, but their pointwise limit is constant red. Thus finite satisfiability does not by itself produce a simultaneous coloring through the closed-set compactness argument. The displayed example explains the exact topological failure, not a counterexample to the problem.

Third extension attempt: find a matching of points such that every A_i contains one matching edge, then color the ends oppositely. Countable families have such a matching by the fresh-pair proof. Maximality of an arbitrary matching is insufficient: a remaining A_i can meet many matching edges in exactly one endpoint without containing a whole edge. The condition |A_i intersect A_j|!=1 applies to original sets A_j, not to chosen matching edges, so it cannot be substituted for that missing condition. Replacing every point of a prospective bad family by a pair makes all finite intersections even, but also gives a universal coloring by opposite twins; therefore this inflation cannot yield a counterexample. The unpaid lemma is a globally consistent pairing or recoloring principle for arbitrary indexing, or an actual uncolorable family with all intersections finite and never singleton. Neither is proved here.
